AI.conclusion: UBC 1052 represents a rare candidate for an inward-migrated open cluster in the inner disc with distinctive chemical features, making it valuable for chemical-tagging searches of dispersed member stars and understanding inner-disc cluster dynamics.

title: The environmental imprint on molecular layering in the dusty streamer of M512
comment: Accepted for publication as a Letter in Astronomy & Astrophysics Section "6. Interstellar and circumstellar matter"
summary: Protostellar streamers are elongated structures that channel material from larger scale onto disks, influencing their physical and chemical evolution. The M512 protostar in Orion/Lynds 1641 hosts one of the most massive and extended streamer discovered so far, offering a unique opportunity to study these processes. We investigate the morphology, chemistry, and origin of this streamer,and its potential impact on the protostellar disk. Using archival ALMA observations of C18O, DCO+, N2D+, and HCO+, we compare their spatial distributions through moment maps and spatial profiles. The streamer shows clear chemical stratification: C18O lies on the western side of the protostar, N2D+ is farther out to the east, and DCO+ is in the middle. This suggests that the structure has been shaped by environmental effects rather than tracing a single coherent infalling flow, with only the densest gas near the protostar likely to accrete onto the disk. Overall, the bulk of the streamer reflects the physical and chemical imprint of the surrounding cloud, highlighting the importance of environmental shaping in interpreting streamer-disk connections and their role in disk growth.

AI.tldr: The M512 protostellar streamer in Orion/Lynds 1641 shows chemical stratification indicating environmental shaping rather than coherent infall, with only dense gas near the protostar likely to accrete onto the disk.
AI.motivation: To investigate the morphology, chemistry, and origin of the massive M512 protostellar streamer in Orion/Lynds 1641, and understand its potential impact on the protostellar disk.
AI.method: Used archival ALMA observations of C18O, DCO+, N2D+, and HCO+ molecular lines, comparing their spatial distributions through moment maps and spatial profiles to analyze chemical stratification.
AI.result: The streamer shows clear chemical stratification: C18O on the western side, N2D+ farther out to the east, and DCO+ in between, suggesting environmental shaping rather than a single coherent infalling flow.
AI.conclusion: Only the densest gas near the protostar is likely to accrete onto the disk; the bulk of the streamer reflects environmental cloud imprint, highlighting the importance of environmental shaping in streamer-disk connections and disk growth.

title: Scale-dependent surface and volume density properties of filaments in molecular clouds
comment: 23 pages, 17 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present a systematic analysis of scale-dependent properties of filamentary structures in seven nearby molecular clouds -- Taurus, Ophiuchus, Perseus, Orion A, California, IC 5146, and Vela C -- using the multiscale extraction method getsf. Alongside the usual surface density profiles $Σ(r)$, we derive volume density profiles $ρ(r)$ for a large sample of filaments, providing new observational constraints on their three-dimensional structure. Filament widths increase systematically with spatial scale, following power laws $\tilde{H} \propto Y^{0.50}$ and $\tilde{h} \propto Y^{0.37}$, with distributions spanning $\sim$ 0.01--1 pc across all scales, challenging the notion of a universal filament width of $\sim$ 0.1 pc. The median volume density slopes $\tildeβ \approx 2.1$--$2.4$ are systematically lower than the value $β= 4$ expected for an isothermal cylinder in hydrostatic equilibrium. Volume density contrasts are substantially higher than surface density contrasts ($\tilde{C}_ρ \approx 17$--$52$ vs. $\tilde{C}_Σ \approx 1.1$--$2.7$), confirming that filaments are substantially more prominent in three dimensions than their projected appearance suggests. The median linear densities of filaments increase linearly with spatial scale, $\tildeΛ \propto Y$, with the fraction of supercritical filaments ($Λ> 15\,M_\odot$ pc$^{-1}$) increasing strongly with scale and varying widely among clouds, from $\sim$ 7% in Taurus and Ophiuchus to $\sim$ 54% in Vela C, broadly consistent with the known star formation activity of the clouds. Measured filament widths and slopes depend systematically on angular resolution and distance, highlighting the importance of accounting for resolution bias in comparative filament studies.

AI.tldr: Filament widths in molecular clouds scale with spatial scale following power laws, challenging the universal 0.1 pc width concept; volume density slopes are shallower than isothermal cylinder predictions, and supercritical filament fractions correlate with star formation activity.
AI.motivation: To systematically analyze scale-dependent properties of filamentary structures in nearby molecular clouds and provide new observational constraints on their three-dimensional structure, challenging previous assumptions about universal filament widths.
AI.method: Used the multiscale extraction method getsf to analyze seven nearby molecular clouds (Taurus, Ophiuchus, Perseus, Orion A, California, IC 5146, and Vela C), deriving both surface density profiles Σ(r) and volume density profiles ρ(r) for a large sample of filaments.
AI.result: Filament widths increase systematically with spatial scale following power laws (H̃ ∝ Y^0.50 and h̃ ∝ Y^0.37), spanning ~0.01-1 pc across all scales. Volume density slopes β̃ ≈ 2.1-2.4 are systematically lower than β=4 expected for isothermal cylinders. Volume density contrasts are substantially higher than surface density contrasts (C̃_ρ ≈ 17-52 vs. C̃_Σ ≈ 1.1-2.7). Supercritical filament fractions vary widely among clouds (7% in Taurus/Ophiuchus to 54% in Vela C), correlating with star formation activity.
AI.conclusion: Filament properties are scale-dependent rather than universal, with widths increasing systematically with spatial scale. Filaments are more prominent in three dimensions than their projected appearance suggests. The fraction of supercritical filaments correlates with cloud star formation activity, and resolution bias must be accounted for in comparative filament studies.

title: Global m=1 slow mode in near-Keplerian self-gravitating torus: applications to stellar nuclear disks and AGN molecular tori
summary: Global m=1 asymmetries are observed in many self-gravitating astrophysical systems and are often interpreted as large-scale slow modes in near-Keplerian potentials. Prominent examples include eccentric nuclear disks in galactic centres, such as the double nucleus of M31. However, the origin and long-term stability of such modes remain unclear. We investigate the evolution and stability of a collisionless, self-gravitating torus orbiting a dominant central mass, aiming to determine whether a slow non-axisymmetric (m=1) mode can arise spontaneously. We perform direct N-body simulations exploring different torus-to-central mass ratios and initial conditions. The calculations use the high-order Hermite GPU integrator (φ-GPU), allowing us to follow long-term evolution with many particles. We find that a global slow m=1 mode forms spontaneously from initially axisymmetric configurations. The lopsided structure is sustained by coherent apsidal alignment and persists over secular timescales. Its maintenance requires nonlinear coupling of low-order modes, including the m=3 component, as well as a sufficient vertical thickness of the torus. As a result of the long-lived overdensity, the central mass is displaced from the system barycenter. These results provide a framework for understanding eccentric nuclear disks, such as those in M31 and NGC4486B, as well as molecular tori in AGNs, and suggest that such asymmetries may produce observable offsets of the central supermassive black hole.

AI.tldr: Global m=1 asymmetries form spontaneously in self-gravitating tori around central masses, explaining eccentric nuclear disks and suggesting observable black hole offsets.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin and long-term stability of global m=1 asymmetries observed in self-gravitating astrophysical systems like eccentric nuclear disks in galactic centers (e.g., M31's double nucleus), which are often interpreted as large-scale slow modes in near-Keplerian potentials.
AI.method: Direct N-body simulations using the high-order Hermite GPU integrator (φ-GPU) to study collisionless, self-gravitating tori orbiting a dominant central mass. Explored different torus-to-central mass ratios and initial conditions, following long-term evolution with many particles.
AI.result: A global slow m=1 mode forms spontaneously from initially axisymmetric configurations. The lopsided structure is sustained by coherent apsidal alignment and persists over secular timescales. Its maintenance requires nonlinear coupling of low-order modes (including m=3) and sufficient vertical thickness of the torus. The central mass becomes displaced from the system barycenter due to the long-lived overdensity.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a framework for understanding eccentric nuclear disks (M31, NGC4486B) and molecular tori in AGNs, suggesting such asymmetries may produce observable offsets of central supermassive black holes from system barycenters.

title: Do little red dots really form a distinct class of astronomical objects?
summary: JWST observations have identified a class of enigmatic sources known as "Little Red Dots" (LRDs). These have been interpreted as a distinct class of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and host galaxies, potentially involving "quasi-stars" or Black Hole stars (BH*). However, two questions remain: is there a clear discontinuity between LRDs and field galaxies, and do LRDs form a homogeneous population? In this work, we address these issues by introducing a continuous metric to evaluate the "LRDness" of galaxies. We measure their compactness ($δ_{compact}$), the sharpness of the V-shaped spectral energy distribution ($δ_{v-shape}$), and the strength of the broad Balmer line emission. We apply this approach to a sample of ~48,000 galaxies with photometric and ~5,000 with spectroscopic information, selected over ~750 arcmin^2. We find that V-shape prominence correlates strongly with morphology without a clear transition at common LRD selection thresholds: the fraction of compact galaxies rises continuously with V-shape intensity. Similarly, broad H$α$ strength increases with both V-shape sharpness and compactness. The [N II] deficit is not an exclusive feature of LRDs but a global property of compact, metal-poor galaxies. Only the 3% most extreme LRDs present a prominent Balmer break (>3) of potentially non-stellar origin. LRDs and non-LRDs follow similar trends in the evolution of the Balmer decrement with V-shape sharpness, suggesting a shared physical origin, likely dust attenuation. Estimated dust masses (~4-7 x 10^4 M_{sun}) and luminosities are low enough to account for their non-detection by ALMA. We conclude that most LRDs do not represent a separate class of objects, but rather the extreme tail of a continuous distribution of galaxies and broad H$α$ emitters, consistent with a classical broad line region and dust attenuation.

AI.tldr: LRDs are not a distinct class but represent the extreme tail of a continuous distribution of galaxies, with their properties (compactness, V-shaped SED, broad Hα) varying continuously rather than showing clear discontinuities.
AI.motivation: To determine whether Little Red Dots (LRDs) form a distinct class of AGN/host galaxies or represent the extreme end of a continuous distribution, and to assess if LRDs constitute a homogeneous population.
AI.method: Developed a continuous metric to quantify "LRDness" based on compactness (δ_compact), V-shaped SED sharpness (δ_v-shape), and broad Balmer line emission strength. Applied to ~48,000 photometric and ~5,000 spectroscopic galaxies over ~750 arcmin².
AI.result: No clear discontinuity between LRDs and field galaxies; properties vary continuously. V-shape prominence correlates strongly with morphology. Broad Hα strength increases with both V-shape sharpness and compactness. [N II] deficit is not exclusive to LRDs but a property of compact, metal-poor galaxies. Only 3% most extreme LRDs show prominent Balmer breaks (>3) of potentially non-stellar origin. LRDs and non-LRDs follow similar dust attenuation trends. Dust masses (~4-7×10⁴ M☉) and luminosities explain ALMA non-detections.
AI.conclusion: Most LRDs do not constitute a separate class but represent the extreme tail of a continuous distribution of galaxies and broad Hα emitters, consistent with classical broad line regions and dust attenuation.
